blurb: Turbofans, ramjets, scramjets, rockets, ion and Hall thrusters, nuclear thermal, and detonation engines — compared on thrust, specific impulse, speed regime, and maturity.
question: What should push this vehicle, and how fast and how far?
title: Propulsion Systems: A Practical Reference
lede: Every propulsion choice is a trade between thrust and efficiency, and the speed regime decides which end of that trade you get. This guide covers {{N_ENTRIES}} propulsion technologies across seven classes, with thrust class, specific impulse, operating regime, maturity, and the cost of an engine.

facets.label: Regime
facets.tip: Where the engine actually works: subsonic flight, supersonic flight, hypersonic flight (roughly Mach 5+), launch and boost through the atmosphere, or in-space maneuvering and transfer.

facets.label: Thrust
facets.tip: Thrust per unit at typical installed sizes. Micro (<1 N) · Small (1 N–10 kN) · Medium (10–200 kN) · Large (200 kN–2 MN) · Heavy (2 MN+). Families that scale across sizes carry a span.

facets.label: Isp
facets.tip: Specific impulse: seconds of 1-lb thrust per pound of propellant burned. Air-breathing engines score in the thousands because they do not carry their oxidizer, so compare them to each other rather than to rockets. Systems with no propellant flow of their own — sails, battery-electric and fuel-cell aircraft — carry no Isp tag.

facets.label: Maturity
facets.tip: Mature = decades of fleet service · In service = fielded and flying now · Emerging = flight-tested or in early production · Research = ground tests and programs, nothing operational.

facets.label: Cost
facets.tip: Directional cost of one engine or thruster at typical production quantity, not the cost of the program that developed it. Expendable and mass-produced units sit at the low end; large flight-qualified engines at the high end.
